slides: In psychometric thinking, we also solve by understanding.

slides.say: We have one more way to solve, and we'll use it all through the course. We call it understanding.

When we solve by understanding, we don't start with a long calculation. We use rules we already know about positive and negative numbers, size, even and odd numbers, and order. We check which rule fits the given conditions. Then we use it to decide what must be true.
at: we don't start with a long calculation

slides.say: You already used it in the very first question of this topic. When we square a number that ends in six, the result ends in six. That's a rule about the last digit, so we ruled out two choices without doing the full multiplication.
at: When we square a number that ends in six

slides.say: Here's the first example. a is negative and b is positive. Which of the following is necessarily negative?
at: a is negative and b is positive

slides.say: Look at a times b. Remember the rule for multiplying: different signs give a negative. a is negative and b is positive, so a times b is always negative, for every a and b that fit.
at: so a times b is always negative

slides.say: Why not the others? b minus a. Taking away any negative number is like adding its opposite, so b minus a is positive plus positive. It's positive.
a squared times b. a times a has the same signs, so it's positive. And positive times positive b is positive.

And a plus b can be positive, negative, or zero. It depends on whether the positive amount or the negative amount has the bigger absolute value. The given conditions don't decide that. So a plus b isn't necessarily negative.
at: So a plus b isn't necessarily

slides.say: The second example. n is an integer. Which is necessarily odd, four n plus three, or n plus three?
Four n is two times two n, and two times an integer is always even. That's the definition of even.
Even plus three is always odd, because even plus one is odd, and adding two more keeps it odd. So four n plus three is odd for every integer n.
But n plus three depends on n. If n is even, it's odd, and if n is odd, it's even. So it isn't necessarily odd.
And the third example. x is between zero and one. Which is bigger, x, or x squared?
at: x is between zero and one

slides.say: x squared is x times x. So it's x, times a number smaller than one.
at: x squared is x times x

slides.say: When we multiply a positive number by a positive number smaller than one, we take only a part of it, so it gets smaller. So x squared is smaller than x.
We can check with one number. A third times a third is a ninth, and a ninth is smaller than a third. The check agrees with the rule.
How is this different from an insight? With an insight, we notice something special in that question. There isn't one fixed procedure we can repeat for every insight question.
Understanding uses general rules, the same ones again and again, in many questions. That's why it's worth learning as a method.

So when do we solve by understanding? When they ask what must be true, what could be true, or what cannot be true. And when the question is about signs, about which number is bigger, about even and odd, or about order.
at: When they ask what must be true
And when the question is about signs

slides.say: Later in the course you'll use it a lot. Most questions on absolute value, on the number line and on integers are solved by understanding.
at: Later in the course you'll use it a lot

slides.say: And the trap. Use only a rule that's always true. If you're not sure, plug in numbers as a safety net. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
